extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, and university press/typographical staff
extracted.subtask_description: A university-press Manual of Style giving typographical and composition rules (capitalization, use of italics, punctuation, divisions, footnotes, indexing, tabular work, technical terms, specimen types, and practical hints) intended to guide authors, editors, proofreaders and compositors. Focus here is the sections on capitalization and italics and their examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1. Proper nouns and adjectives derived from proper nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize proper nouns and adjectives derived from proper nouns (e.g., George, America, Elizabethan, French).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize verbs derived from proper names (e.g., to boycott, to christianize, to pasteurize). Examples given: George, North America, Englishman; Elizabethan, French.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2. Epithets used as substitutes for proper names, or affixed to a name
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize epithets used in place of proper names or affixed to a name (e.g., the Pretender, Richard the Lion-hearted, Alexander the Great).

rubrics_metrics.name: 3. Particles in French names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize French particles like 'Le', 'La', 'De', 'Du' when the particle stands without a Christian name or title preceding; do not when preceded by such name or title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Le Bossu, La Torre, La Rochelle, De Coligny, D'Aubign�; but: Ren� le Bossu, Miguel de la Torre, Thomas d'Aubign�. Note: Always capitalize 'Van' in Dutch names; never capitalize 'von' in German names (Stephen Van Rensselaer; Hugo von Martius).

rubrics_metrics.name: 4. Generic terms forming part of geographical names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize generic terms that form an integral part of geographical names (e.g., Atlantic Ocean, Mississippi River, Rocky Mountains).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize such words when they are merely descriptive additions (e.g., the river Elbe, the desert of Sahara, the island of Madagascar). Provides lists of geographic generic nouns to capitalize in singular form when immediately following a name and guidance for plural usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5. Adjectives and nouns distinguishing definite regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize adjectives and nouns used singly or in conjunction to distinguish definite regions or parts of the world (e.g., Old World, Western Hemisphere, North Pole, the East, the Orient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not, as a rule, capitalize adjectives derived from such names or nouns simply designating direction or point of compass (e.g., oriental customs, northern Europe, the southern states). Exception noted: Northman = Scandinavian.

rubrics_metrics.name: 6. Generic terms for political divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize terms for political divisions when they are an organic part of the name, when used as an integral part with 'of', when used singly as accepted designation, or when part of a fanciful/popular appellation used as a real geographical name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Holy Roman Empire, Department of the Lakes, the Union, Celestial Empire. Do not capitalize when standing alone or with 'of' preceding (e.g., empire of Russia, state of Illinois), with limited exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7. Numbered political divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize ordinal-numbered political subdivisions or divisions (e.g., Eleventh Congressional District, First Ward, Second Precinct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 100 for related numbering guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8. Names of thoroughfares, parks, squares, buildings, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of streets, parks, squares, blocks, buildings and similar proper names (e.g., Drexel Avenue, Trafalgar Square, Monadnock Block, White House).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize general designations like 'courthouse', 'post-office', 'library' except in connection with the name of the place in which they are located.

rubrics_metrics.name: 9. Names of political parties, religious denominations, and schools
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of political parties, religious denominations/sects, philosophical/literary/artistic schools and their adherents when referring to specific organizations/movements (e.g., Republican, Christian, Catholic, Romantic movement, Symbolic school of painters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize these words when used in a general sense or to indicate trend/spirit (e.g., republican form of government, evangelic spirit, epicurean tastes). Examples and exceptions provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: 10. Names of monastic orders and their members
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of monastic orders and their members (e.g., Black Friars, Dominican, Jesuit).

rubrics_metrics.name: 11. Proper (official) titles of organizations and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize full official names of social, religious, educational, political, commercial and industrial organizations and institutions (e.g., Union League Club, Smithsonian Institution, State University of Iowa, Associated Press).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize generic terms when used to designate a class or when standing alone, except to avoid ambiguity or where clearly used in place of the true name (examples provided: 'the club' vs 'the Hall [Tammany]'). See rule 49 for institutional divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12. Names of legislative, judiciary, administrative bodies and departments
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of specific legislative, judiciary, administrative bodies and government departments and their branches when specifically applied (e.g., Congress, Parliament, Supreme Court of the United States, Department of the Interior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize general, paraphrastic or incomplete designations (e.g., the legislature of the state, the council, the department).

rubrics_metrics.name: 13. Ordinals for dynasties, congressional sessions, regiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize ordinals used to designate Egyptian dynasties, sessions of Congress, names of regiments, and similar contexts (e.g., the Eighteenth Dynasty, the Fifty-third Congress, the Second Illinois Regiment Band).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 100 for numbering conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 14. Appellations for historical epochs, periods, geological ages
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize commonly accepted names for historical epochs, language/literature periods, and geological ages/strata. 'Age' is capitalized only to avoid ambiguity (e.g., Middle Ages, Renaissance, Pleistocene).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and notes given.

rubrics_metrics.name: 15. Names for important events
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize accepted names of important historical events (e.g., Thirty Years' War, Revolution, War of 1812, Battle of Gettysburg, Peace of Utrecht).

rubrics_metrics.name: 16. Political alliances and historically significant terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize political alliances and secular/ecclesiastical historical terms that through association have become designations for parties or movements (e.g., Protestant League, Holy Alliance, the Roses, Roundheads).

rubrics_metrics.name: 17. Conventions, congresses, expositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of conventions, congresses, expositions, assemblies (e.g., Council of Nicaea, Chicago World's Fair, Westminster Assembly).

rubrics_metrics.name: 18. Titles of specific treaties, acts, laws, bills
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of specific treaties, acts, laws, bills and juridical instruments (e.g., Treaty of Verdun, Declaration of Independence, Magna Carta, Fourteenth Amendment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note on 'the Constitution' capitalized when referring to U.S. Constitution in certain literary or stand-alone contexts; other constitutions often lowercased.

rubrics_metrics.name: 19. Creeds and confessions of faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize formal creeds and confessions of faith (e.g., Apostles' Creed, Nicene Creed, Augsburg Confession, Thirty-nine Articles).

rubrics_metrics.name: 20. Civic and ecclesiastical feast-days
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of civic and ecclesiastical feast days (e.g., Fourth of July, Labor Day, Thanksgiving Day, Easter, Passover).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize 'sabbath' when used as common noun (sabbath = day of rest).

rubrics_metrics.name: 21. Titles, civil and military, and academic degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles preceding names, academic degrees in abbreviated form following names, titles of honor/nobility when referring to specific persons, familiar names applied to specific persons, orders and titles accompanying them; capitalize titles standing alone when referring to existing incumbents (e.g., Queen Victoria, Rear-Admiral Dewey, Timothy Dwight, D.D., LL.D., His Majesty, the Senator, 'The President').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize titles of occupants when following the name, when standing alone (with some exceptions), or when preceded by 'the' and referring generically (e.g., McKinley, president of the United States; the emperor of Germany [not the existing emperor]). See rule 49 and 49's exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 22. Abbreviations like Ph.D., M.P., F.R.G.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize honorific and professional abbreviations consisting of multiple letters and set without spaces between letters (e.g., Ph.D., M.P., F.R.G.S.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See related rules (52, 103, 106). Do not capitalize spelled-out phrases such as 'doctor of philosophy' (unless other rules apply).

rubrics_metrics.name: 23. Single-letter abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize single-letter abbreviations, except for units of measurement and minor literary subdivisions (see related sections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: R.V. (Revised Version), C. (centigrade), L.C.M. (lowest common multiple), H.P. (horse-power), A.U. (Angstrom units).

rubrics_metrics.name: 24. Names and adjectives designating the Supreme Being or Power
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize nouns and adjectives designating the Supreme Being or Power and pronouns referring to the same, when not closely preceded/followed by a distinctive name or when such reference would be ambiguous (e.g., the Almighty, Providence, Father, Son, Holy Ghost).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize derivatives like 'fatherhood', 'messiahship', 'messianic' (but: Christology). Examples and caveats provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: 25. Words with acquired, limited, or special meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize words that have acquired a limited or special meaning in context (e.g., the Doctor's degree, a report of the Master in chancery, a Bachelor's hood, a Freshman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize where the explanatory phrasing has become generic (e.g., the doctorate, a master in chancery).

rubrics_metrics.name: 26. Personified abstract ideas (e.g., 'Nature')
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Nature' and similar terms and abstract ideas when personified (e.g., 'Nature wields her scepter').

rubrics_metrics.name: 27. 'Father' for church father and 'Reformers' for Reformation leaders when ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Father' when used for church Father and 'Reformers' when referring to Reformation leaders whenever the meaning would otherwise be ambiguous (e.g., the Fathers, the Reformers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize where the phrasing is clearly descriptive (e.g., the church reformers of the fifteenth century).

rubrics_metrics.name: 28. The word 'church' in properly cited titles and edifices
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Church' when it forms part of properly cited titles of nationally organized bodies of believers or when part of the name of a particular edifice (e.g., Church of Rome, Church of England, Fifth Avenue Baptist Church).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize 'church' when standing alone in general senses (e.g., the Roman Catholic church), except in exceptional rhetorical antithesis between Church and State where capitalization may be used for emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: 29. Names for the Bible and other sacred books
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles for the Bible and other sacred books and collective names for sacred scripture (e.g., Scriptures, Holy Writ, Koran, Vedas, Mishna).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize adjectives derived from such nouns (e.g., biblical, scriptural, koranic).

rubrics_metrics.name: 30. Versions of the Bible
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of specific Bible versions (e.g., King James's Version, Authorized Version, Revised Version, Septuagint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviations provided (A.V., R.V.).

rubrics_metrics.name: 31. Books and divisions of the Bible and sacred books
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of books and divisions of the Bible and other sacred books when cited (e.g., Old Testament, Exodus, Psalms, Gospel of Luke, Epistle to the Romans, Sermon on the Mount).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize generic words like 'book', 'gospel', 'epistle', 'psalm' in generic references (e.g., the five books of Moses, the first forty psalms). See rule 60 for cross-references.

rubrics_metrics.name: 32. Biblical parables
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of well-known biblical parables (e.g., the parable of the Prodigal Son).

rubrics_metrics.name: 33. Miscellaneous biblical/cultic designations
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize notable biblical terms and group designations (e.g., Last Supper, Eucharist, the Passion, the Twelve, the Seventy, the Golden Rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: 34. First word of a sentence and first word in poetry lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word of a sentence and, in poetry, the first word of each line (except in Greek and Latin poetry where only the first word of a paragraph is capitalized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from English, Greek, Latin poetry given; special treatment for classical verse noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35. First word after a colon when it begins an independent sentence or passage
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word after a colon only when it introduces a complete passage or sentence that would stand independently (e.g., in summarizations or quotations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize when the quotation is immediately connected with what precedes or when the colon signals a dependent explanatory phrase. Examples: capitalized 'It will be seen...' vs not capitalizing 'haste makes waste' in a connected quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 36. First word in enumerated sections with independent clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, capitalize the first word in sections of enumeration if any item contains two or more distinct clauses separated by semicolon/colon/period unless all are dependent on the preceding term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples shown illustrating when to capitalize enumeration items and when not to.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37. Nouns followed by a numeral indicating sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize nouns followed by a numeral indicating order in sequence, particularly Roman numerals (e.g., Room 16, Grade IV, Act I, Vol. I, Book II).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize minor subdivisions like sec., scene i, art. iii, chap. 2(ii) in ordinary usage (see related rules 38/100/237).

rubrics_metrics.name: 38. First word of a cited speech or thought in direct discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word of a cited speech or thought in direct discourse, whether preceded by a colon or comma (e.g., 'Never shall I forget this day').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See cross-references to rule 131 for quotation punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 39. First words following 'Whereas' and 'Resolved' in resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first words following 'Whereas' and 'Resolved' in resolutions (formal capitalization of 'Whereas, It has pleased God...' etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: 40. Exclamations 'O' and 'Oh'
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the exclamations 'O' and 'Oh' (e.g., 'O Lord!', 'Oh, I know not!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 117 for related usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: 41. Principal words in English titles of publications and headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize all principal words (nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs, verbs, first and last words) in English titles of publications and divisions thereof, and in subjects of lectures, toasts, and in certain headings and table heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Men Who Made the Nation; The American College — Its Past and Present. Note that certain bibliographic practices (e.g., Botanical Gazette) may capitalize only first words and proper names.

rubrics_metrics.name: 42. Capitalization in foreign titles
rubrics_metrics.description: In foreign titles follow these rules: (a) Latin: capitalize proper nouns and adjectives derived from them; (b) French, Italian, Spanish, Scandinavian: capitalize proper nouns but not adjectives derived therefrom; (c) German and Danish: capitalize all nouns but not adjectives (except German adjectives derived from persons); (d) Dutch: capitalize all nouns and adjectives derived from proper nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples for each language: De amicitia; Histoire de la lit�rature fran�aise; Geschichte des deutschen Feudalwesens; Gesckldenis det Nederlandsche Volk.

rubrics_metrics.name: 43. Definite article in newspaper/magazine titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not, as a rule, treat the definite article ('the') as part of the title of newspapers and magazines when mentioning them in running text (e.g., the Chicago Tribune, the School Review).

rubrics_metrics.name: 44. Titles of ancient manuscripts (MS, MSS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of ancient manuscripts (e.g., Codex Bemensis, Cod. Canonicianus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 60 for related bibliographic conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 45. Hyphenated compounds in titles
rubrics_metrics.description: In titles with main words capitalized, capitalize all nouns forming parts of hyphenated compounds (e.g., Twentieth-Century Progress; The Economy of High-Speed Trains).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize hyphenated components that are not nouns (examples: Fifty-first Street, 'Lives of Well-known Authors').

rubrics_metrics.name: 46. Scientific (Latin) names in botanical/zoological/paleontological matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize scientific Latin names of divisions/orders/families/genera but not their English derivatives (e.g., Cotylosauria but cotylosaurs; F�idae but felids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Names of species derived from persons or generic names may be capitalized in botanical and zoological contexts; in geological and medical matter species names are not capitalized. Examples provided (Felis leo, Cocos nucifera, Parkinsonia Torreyana). See rule 71.

rubrics_metrics.name: 47. Names and epithets of peoples, races, tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names and epithets of peoples, races and tribes (e.g., Kafir, Negro, Hottentot, Makassar).

rubrics_metrics.name: 48. Astronomical bodies in our solar system
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of bodies in our solar system except the words 'sun', 'earth', 'moon', 'stars' (e.g., the Milky Way, the Great Bear, Saturn).

rubrics_metrics.name: 49. University of Chicago divisions, departments, officers and courses (institutional capitals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize divisions, departments, officers, and courses of study of the University of Chicago in official work (e.g., the School of Education, the Department of Anthropology, the Board of Trustees, the President).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lower-case generically (e.g., the division, the department) unless in official/administrative contexts. Examples illustrate usage for courses and terms (Autumn Quarter vs a quarter).

rubrics_metrics.name: 50. Capitals and small capitals in letter datelines and salutations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use capitals and small capitals for names of town and state in the dateline and for salutatory phrases and signatures in letters; set these in specific typesetting positions and sizes (dateline, signature conventions described).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and typographical layout guidance: Chicago, Ill., January 1, 1911; 'My dear Mr. Smith:' set flush followed by a colon, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 51. 'Whereas', 'Note', 'Section' in resolutions/notes/constitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Whereas' in resolutions; 'Note' in notes (not footnotes) which should be followed by a period and dash; 'Section' introducing paragraphs in constitutions/by-laws followed by number should be capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviation practice for subsequent 'section' uses (Section 1 then Sec. 2, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: 52. Small capitals for A.M., P.M., B.C., A.D.
rubrics_metrics.description: Set A.M., P.M., B.C., A.D. in small capitals without spaces between letters (e.g., 11:30 A.M.; 53 B.C., 1906 A.D.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-references to rules 22, 103, 106, 219.

rubrics_metrics.name: 53. Lower-case for commonized proper names and derived verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case initial letters for words of common usage originally proper names whose origin is obscured and generally for verbs derived from proper names (e.g., utopia, bohemian, boycott, italicize, christianize).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed showing anglicized forms that are lower-cased.

rubrics_metrics.name: 54. Lower-case for minor literary subdivisions in references
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case for minor subdivisions in literary references and their abbreviations (chapter, section, page, article, verse, line, note; abbreviations chap., sec., p., art., vs., l., n.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 37, 110, 237 for cross-reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: 55. Units of measurement abbreviations in lower-case
rubrics_metrics.description: Set units of measurement in lower-case abbreviations (e.g., h.=hour, min.=minute, sec.=second, lb.=pound, oz.=ounce, yd.=yard, ft.=foot).

rubrics_metrics.name: 56. Italic side-heads capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: In italic side-heads, set all words in lower-case except the first word and proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 172 and 280 for further detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: 57. First word of a quotation joined to preceding text (no cap)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not capitalize the first word of a quotation which is immediately connected with what precedes, even if it begins a sentence in the original; exceptions and illustrations cross-referenced to rules 35 and 131.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided earlier for contrasting treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: 58. Italicize words/phrases for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use italics to lend emphasis or importance to words or phrases (e.g., 'This was, however, not the case').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate emphasis in prose and rhetorical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 59. Italicize foreign words and short foreign passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words and phrases from foreign languages inserted into English text and not incorporated into English; also (as a rule) single sentences or brief passages from foreign language not long enough to call for reduced type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Darwinian Weltanschauung', 'coup d'etat', 'De gustibus non est disputandum'. Do not italicize foreign titles preceding names or names of foreign institutions/places commonly used without English equivalents (e.g., P�re Lagrange, Reichstag, Champs Elys�es). Also do not italicize foreign words sufficiently anglicized (e.g., percent, menu, naive, resume). A long list of commonly italicized foreign terms is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: 60. Italicize titles of publications, books, plays, periodicals and newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize titles of publications — books (including plays, essays, cycles of poems printed separately), pamphlets, treatises, documents, and periodicals, and in newspapers/periodicals italicize the name of the city when it is integral to the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Principles of Sociology; A Midsummer Night's Dream; the Independent, the Modern Language Review, the Chicago Tribune. Note: Botanical Gazette uses italics in text but roman in footnotes; its own name printed in caps and small caps. (Rule continues beyond truncated excerpt.)
